Empirical Research Plan – Police Presence and Property Crime in Buenos Aires After the 1994 AMIA Attack  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension.

Rationale  
• The AMIA bombing produced a sudden, security-driven reallocation of police that was unrelated to contemporaneous neighborhood-level crime trends.  
• We observe multiple neighborhoods (i) over time (t) both before and after the shock, allowing us to compare crime trends in areas that received an exogenous police boost (treated) with those that did not (control).  
• A staggered or continuous-intensity DID can be augmented with an event study to test for pre-trends and to trace dynamics.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
Treated_i = 1 if neighborhood i experienced a non-trivial jump in police intensity following 18 July 1994. Operational definitions:  
a. Binary: ΔPolice_i ≥ median(ΔPolice) across all neighborhoods in the first two post-attack weeks.  
b. Continuous: ΔPolice_it (officers per 1,000 inhabitants). Main results use the binary DID; robustness uses the continuous dose-response.

Control group  
Neighborhoods with little or no change in police presence (lowest quartile of ΔPolice). They represent the counterfactual trend in absence of the surge.

Treatment timing  
Event date = 18 July 1994. Post_t = 1 for all t ≥ 18 July 1994; 0 before.

(Optional IV for robustness)  
First stage: Predicted post-attack deployment based on distance to “potential Jewish or governmental targets,” arguing that proximity, not crime, drove the allocation.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: Prior to 18 July 1994 the property-crime trends of treated and control neighborhoods evolved similarly. Plausibility: allocation of police before the attack was routine and unrelated to unobserved diverging trends. Testable via pre-period event-study coefficients.  
A2. No anticipation: Neighborhoods did not predict the bombing; thus behavior or policing did not adjust before 18 July 1994. Highly plausible.  
A3. Stable composition: Neighborhood boundaries and reporting mechanisms remain unchanged throughout the window (±6 months). Plausible given the short horizon.  
A4. No interference/spillovers: Extra police in treated areas do not simply displace crime into controls (or siphon police away). Potentially violated; addressed below.  
A5. Time-variant confounders: No other city-wide shocks differentially affect treated vs. control after the bombing (e.g., economic shock localized to certain barrios). Use neighborhood and day fixed effects and controls (unemployment, weather) to mitigate.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Crime displacement / police subtraction from controls.  
• Test: Check whether police counts fall in control areas post-attack.  
• Mitigation: Construct net-police variable; include neighborhood-specific linear trends; estimate spatial lag models; or exclude immediate geographic neighbors.

T2. Endogenous deployment related to unobserved crime risk (e.g., wealthier Jewish neighborhoods already safer).  
• Mitigation: Control for pre-attack mean property-crime level, socio-economic variables, and fixed effects.  
• Robustness: Instrument with distance to potential terror targets.

T3. Measurement error in crime reports (more police may raise reporting).  
• Use victimization survey data if available, or contrast property crimes that are almost always reported (auto-theft) with low-report crimes (petty theft).  
• Estimate models on non-property crimes unlikely to be affected by policing (e.g., domestic violence) as falsification tests.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
#-----------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)  # fast data wrangling
library(lubridate)
library(fixest)      # high-dim FE regressions
library(ggplot2)

#-----------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
crime  <- fread("crime_daily_neigh.csv")        # neighborhood-day level
police <- fread("police_deployment.csv")        # same granularity
socio  <- fread("socio_neighborhood.csv")       # time-invariant controls

#-----------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Variable Construction
data <- merge(crime, police, by = c("neigh_id","date"))
data <- merge(data,  socio,  by = "neigh_id")

# Date variables
data[, post := as.integer(date >= "1994-07-18")]

# Construct ΔPolice around the event (pre-period = 1 July–17 July)
base_police <- data[date %between% c("1994-07-01","1994-07-17"),
                    .(base_police = mean(police_officers)),
                    by = neigh_id]

data <- merge(data, base_police, by = "neigh_id")
data[, delta_police := police_officers - base_police]

# Define Treatment (binary top-50%)
first2w <- data[date %between% c("1994-07-18","1994-07-31"),
                .(mean_delta = mean(delta_police)),
                by = neigh_id]

cutoff <- quantile(first2w$mean_delta, .5)     # median
treated_ids <- first2w[mean_delta >= cutoff, neigh_id]
data[, treated := as.integer(neigh_id %in% treated_ids)]

# DID interaction
data[, treat_post := treated * post]

# Outcome
data[, prop_crime_rate := property_crimes / population * 1000]

#-----------------------------------------------
# 3. Main Specification
# y_it = β * (treated_i × post_t) + α_i + γ_t + ε_it
did_mod <- feols(prop_crime_rate ~ treat_post | neigh_id + date,
                 data = data, cluster = 'neigh_id')
summary(did_mod)

#-----------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-Study (Lead/Lag dummies)
data[, rel_day := as.numeric(date - as.Date("1994-07-18"))]
for(k in -30:30) data[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(rel_day == k) * treated]

leadlag_vars <- paste0("D", -30:30)[-31]  # drop D0 as omitted
es_mod <- feols(prop_crime_rate ~ ..leadlag_vars | neigh_id + date,
                data = data, cluster = 'neigh_id')
iplot(es_mod)

#-----------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: Poisson count model
pois_mod <- feglm(property_crimes ~ treat_post | neigh_id + date,
                  data = data, family = poisson(),
                  cluster = "neigh_id")
summary(pois_mod)
```

6. Expected Results  
Economic theory (deterrence) predicts β < 0: more officers lower property crime. Prior empirical elasticities suggest −0.3 to −0.5 elasticity. With an average post-attack increase of ~30 % in officers, I expect a 10–15 % decline in daily property-crime incidents in treated neighborhoods (β ≈ −0.02 to −0.03 crimes per 1,000 residents).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1: Parallel pre-trends ………………… 1  
C2: No anticipation ……………………… 1  
C3: No spillovers/interference ………… 0.5  
C4: Exogeneity of treatment …………… 0.5  
C5: Stable composition / measurement … 1  
Total = 4/5 – overall credible but spillovers and endogenous siting remain partial concerns.

-------------------------------------------------------------
